subject: SpaceX Starship Flight 15
title: SpaceX Starship catch: Ship caught by tower arms after orbit, a first
answer: On Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, SpaceX caught its Starship upper stage with the launch tower's mechanical arms at Starbase, Texas, about 22 hours after liftoff. It was the first time a Starship returning from space had been captured. The Super Heavy booster was lost in the Gulf of Mexico.
in_the_news: Catching the ship, not just the booster, is the key step toward a fully reusable rocket, which SpaceX says will sharply cut launch costs and which NASA is counting on for its Moon landings.
body:
The 15th full-scale Starship flight lifted off Friday afternoon, Nov. 13, and was only the program's second trip to orbit. The ship reached an altitude of about 165 miles, circled Earth 14 times, compared with one or two laps on the previous mission, and released 26 Starlink satellites. It then came back through the atmosphere, flipped upright and settled into the tower's "chopstick" arms with its engines still firing. SpaceX said the heat shield appeared to hold up well, and Elon Musk posted that "Ship 42 looks great!" NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman called it "almost magic."

The booster did not fare as well. Its engines shut down too early on the way back, its guidance system triggered a self-destruct, and the wreckage fell into the Gulf of Mexico, where the area has been marked off with buoys. Engineers are investigating. SpaceX had caught Super Heavy boosters three times since October 2024, so the novelty this time was the upper stage.

Starship stands about 407 feet tall and is the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown. SpaceX's Falcon 9 already reuses its first stage, but its second stage is thrown away; recovering both halves of Starship is what could make flights far cheaper and faster to turn around. SpaceX expects to begin Starship launches from Kennedy Space Center in Florida within the next few months.

faq.q: What did SpaceX catch this time?
faq.a: The Starship upper stage, the part that goes to orbit. It was caught by the launch tower's arms after 14 orbits. Earlier catches were of the Super Heavy booster only.

faq.q: What happened to the Super Heavy booster?
faq.a: Its engines stopped too soon during the return, a self-destruct was triggered, and it fell into the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX is investigating.
A rocket that can be fully reused, like an airliner, could cut the cost of each launch dramatically. That is central to SpaceX's plans for Starlink, the Moon and Mars.

faq.q: What does this mean for NASA's Moon missions?
faq.a: NASA is paying SpaceX billions to land Artemis astronauts on the Moon with Starship. Artemis III will practice docking in Earth orbit, and NASA is targeting Artemis IV, the first crewed landing since Apollo, for as early as 2028.
